title: The emerald
hookLine: is an emerald worse if no one praises it? (Meditations 4.20)
carry: an honest answer in an empty room

cards: Deep in a mountain in Colombia, there's an emerald nobody has found. It has been green for millions of years in the dark. No jeweler has held it to the light.
No one has said, oh, look at that. Is it any less green? Marcus Aurelius asked almost exactly that question, in the entry right after the one on fame.
Yesterday was about being remembered. This one is quieter: whether a good thing needs to be seen at all. Today: the emerald.

teach.b: Everything beautiful, Marcus writes in the twentieth entry of book four, is beautiful on its own, and complete in itself. Praise is no part of it. A thing isn't made worse or better by being praised.

teach.h: AN EMERALD, A LYRE, A FLOWER.
teach.b: Is an emerald made worse, he asks, if it isn't praised? What about gold, or ivory, or purple dye? A lyre?
A small knife? A flower? A shrub?
You can almost picture him glancing around the room. None of these changes color when someone walks past without comment.

That holds for objects and works of art, he says, and even more for what is truly beautiful: law, truth, kindness, modesty. Which of these is beautiful because it's praised, or spoiled because it's blamed?

An honest answer given in an empty room is just as honest. A kindness nobody saw is just as kind. After doing something good, it's easy to wait a little for the reaction: the text back, the thank-you, the like.
When it doesn't come, the good thing seems to dim. Marcus says it didn't dim.

teach.h: IT WAS WHOLE BEFORE ANYONE LOOKED.
teach.b: It was finished, and green, and whole, before anyone looked.
That's not an argument against thanking people. Gratitude is a good of its own. It's an argument against needing it, against letting the value of your work sit in someone else's hands.

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes recall the emerald of Meditations 4.20 after doing something good, letting it stand without checking for anyone's reaction.

o: a jewel Marcus wore to show his rank as emperor
Marcus's sign that good things are whole without praise
a stone the Stoics thought could calm an angry mind

s: Marcus says praise makes a good thing a little better
he says a thing is made neither worse nor better by being praised.
Marcus lists a lyre and a small knife beside the emerald
along with gold, ivory, purple, a flower and a shrub.
Marcus says we shouldn't thank people
his point is about needing praise, not about giving gratitude.

games.q: you cooked a careful dinner. everyone eats it and talks about something else. what fits Meditations 4.20?
o: ask them outright if they liked it.
decide not to bother next time.
let it be good, whole, without the praise.
games.why: Marcus: is an emerald worse if no one praises it? the dinner was good before anyone said a word.

practice: Look at one ordinary thing near you, a cup, a plant, your own hand, the way Marcus looks at his emerald: nobody admiring it, complete on its own.
Then think of one good thing in your day that went by without a word, a meal, a job done right, a patient reply. Set it beside the cup: both whole, neither waiting.

wordCard.voice: The emerald. Marcus asks whether an emerald is worse if no one praises it: what's good is complete in itself, praised or not. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'emerald': the stone Marcus asks about in 4.20, and the root of the English word.

carryVoice: Your line: an honest answer in an empty room. Green in the dark is still green. That's day five hundred fifty-seven.
